# Unit 6 Summary {.unnumbered}

Every probability symbol, rule, simulation step, and counting tool from Unit 6 in one place. Use it while you work on the review.

:::{.guided-notes-link}
[Printable summary](/handouts/Unit_6/Unit_6_Summary.pdf){target="_blank"} - these tables on two pages, to print and keep.

### Probability Symbols

| Symbol | Read it as | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $P(A)$ | "the probability of $A$" | How likely $A$ is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). |
| $P(\text{not } A)$ | "the probability of not $A$" | The {{< glink complement >}}: $A$ does **not** happen. Some books write $P(A^C)$. |
| $A \cup B$ | "$A$ {{< glink union >}} $B$" or "$A$ or $B$" | $A$ happens, or $B$ happens, or both. |
| $A \cap B$ | "$A$ {{< glink intersection text="intersect" >}} $B$" or "$A$ and $B$" | $A$ and $B$ both happen (the overlap). |
| $P(A \mid B)$ | "the probability of $A$ **given** $B$" | The probability of $A$ when you know $B$ happened. The bar $\mid$ means "given." |

***

### Probability Rules

| Rule | Formula | When to use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {{< glink probability text="Probability" >}} | $P(A) = \dfrac{\text{number of ways } A \text{ can happen}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}$ | Every outcome is equally likely. | 3 red and 7 blue marbles. Pick one. $P(\text{red}) = \frac{3}{10}$ |
| {{< glink complement text="Complement" >}} | $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$ <br> $P(\text{at least one wrong}) = 1 - P(\text{all right})$ | "Not $A$." Also "at least one" questions. | $P(\text{not red}) = 1 - \frac{3}{10} = \frac{7}{10}$ <br> Guess on 3 questions with 4 choices each: $1 - \frac{1}{64} = \frac{63}{64}$ |
| {{< glink "addition rule" text="Addition rule" >}} | $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ | "Or." Subtract the overlap, because it was counted twice. | 30 students: 12 play soccer ($S$), 10 play basketball ($B$), 4 play both. <br> $P(S \cup B) = \frac{12}{30} + \frac{10}{30} - \frac{4}{30} = \frac{18}{30}$ |
| {{< glink "mutually exclusive" text="Mutually exclusive" >}} | $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ <br> $P(A \cap B) = 0$ | "Or," when $A$ and $B$ cannot both happen. | Roll a number cube. <br> $P(1 \cup 2) = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$ |
| {{< glink "multiplication rule" text="Multiplication rule" >}} | $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$ | "And," for **{{< glink "independent events" text="independent" >}}** events. | Flip a coin and roll a number cube. <br> $P(\text{heads} \cap 6) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12}$ |
| General multiplication rule | $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)$ | "And," for **{{< glink "dependent events" text="dependent" >}}** events. | 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Draw 2. Keep the first one out. <br> $P(\text{red, red}) = \frac{5}{8} \cdot \frac{4}{7} = \frac{5}{14}$ |
| {{< glink "conditional probability" text="Conditional probability" >}} | $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$ <br> {{< glink "two-way table" text="In a table" >}}: <br> $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{\text{number in } A \text{ and } B}{\text{number in } B}$ | You already know $B$ happened. Only look at the $B$ group. | 60 students: 30 play a sport, 20 have a job, 8 do both. <br> $P(\text{job} \mid \text{sport}) = \frac{8}{30} \approx 0.27$ <br> $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{job}) = \frac{8}{20} = 0.40$ |
| Checking independence | $A$ and $B$ are independent if $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$. | Knowing $B$ does not change the probability of $A$. | $P(\text{job}) = \frac{20}{60} \approx 0.33$, but $P(\text{job} \mid \text{sport}) \approx 0.27$. **Not** independent. |

**Independent:** one happening does not change the probability of the other, as in drawing **{{< glink "with replacement" >}}**. **Dependent:** one happening changes it, as in drawing **{{< glink "without replacement" >}}**.

***

### Tree Diagrams

60% of students ride the bus. 25% of bus riders are late. 10% of the others are late.

| 1. Multiply along a path. | 2. Add the paths you want. | 3. Then divide. |
|---|---|---|
| $P(\text{bus} \cap \text{late}) = 0.6 \cdot 0.25 = 0.15$ <br> $P(\text{no bus} \cap \text{late}) = 0.4 \cdot 0.10 = 0.04$ | $P(\text{late}) = 0.15 + 0.04 = 0.19$ | $P(\text{bus} \mid \text{late}) = \frac{0.15}{0.19} \approx 0.79$ |

***

### Simulations

| Idea | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {{< glink "theoretical probability" text="Theoretical probability" >}} | Found by reasoning about equally likely outcomes. | Flip a coin. $P(\text{heads}) = \frac{1}{2}$ |
| {{< glink "experimental probability" text="Experimental probability" >}} | Found by doing trials: $\dfrac{\text{number of times it happened}}{\text{number of trials}}$ | 20 flips, 12 heads: $\frac{12}{20} = 0.6$ |
| {{< glink simulation text="Simulation" >}} | Use random numbers to act out a chance event many times. <br> 1. Assign digits to the outcomes so the probabilities match. <br> 2. Decide what one {{< glink trial >}} is. <br> 3. Run many trials with random digits. <br> 4. Count how often the event happened. | A basketball player makes 70% of her free throws. About how often does she make all 3 of 3 shots? <br> 1. Digits 0 to 6 = make. 7, 8, 9 = miss. <br> 2. One trial = 3 digits (3 shots). <br> 3. Run 10 trials. <br> 4. 4 of the 10 made all 3: $\frac{4}{10} = 0.4$ |
| {{< glink "law of large numbers" text="Law of large numbers" >}} | The more trials you do, the closer the experimental probability usually gets to the theoretical probability. | The theoretical probability of making all 3 shots is $0.7 \cdot 0.7 \cdot 0.7 = 0.343$. With more trials, the simulation would get closer to it. |

***

### Counting

| Tool | Formula | When to use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {{< glink "counting principle" text="Counting principle" >}} | One choice has $m$ options. A second choice has $n$ options: $m \cdot n$ ways. | Count the ways to make both choices. Also when repeats are allowed. | 3 shirts and 4 pairs of pants: $3 \cdot 4 = 12$ outfits <br> 3-letter codes: $26 \cdot 26 \cdot 26 = 17{,}576$ |
| {{< glink factorial text="Factorial" >}} | $n! = n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2) \cdots 2 \cdot 1$ <br> Read "$n$ factorial." $0! = 1$ | Arrange all $n$ things in order. | 4 students sit in 4 chairs in a row: $4! = 24$ ways |
| {{< glink permutation text="Permutation" >}} | ${}_nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!}$ <br> Read "$n$ permute $r$." | **Order matters.** Arrange $r$ of $n$ things. No repeats. | 10 students fill 3 jobs: <br> ${}_{10}P_3 = 10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 = 720$ <br> 3-letter codes: $26 \cdot 25 \cdot 24 = 15{,}600$ |
| {{< glink combination text="Combination" >}} | ${}_nC_r = \dbinom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$ <br> Read "$n$ choose $r$." | **Order does not matter.** Choose $r$ of $n$ things. | A committee of 3 from 5 students: ${}_5C_3 = \frac{5!}{3!\,2!} = 10$ |

**Permutation or combination?** Ask: if I switch the order, is it a different result?

***

### Probability with Counting

$P(\text{event}) = \dfrac{\text{number of ways the event can happen}}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}}$. Count both with the same method.

| Example | 1. Does order matter? | 2. Count all the possible outcomes. | 3. Count the outcomes you want. | 4. Divide. |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A teacher randomly picks 2 students from 5 girls and 4 boys. Find $P(\text{both girls})$. | No. Combination. | ${}_9C_2 = 36$ | ${}_5C_2 = 10$ | $\frac{10}{36} = \frac{5}{18} \approx 0.28$ |
| A club of 10 picks a president and a vice president at random. Find the probability that Ana is president and Ben is vice president. | Yes (different jobs). Permutation. | ${}_{10}P_2 = 90$ | 1 | $\frac{1}{90}$ |
